Why interviews pick the wrong people

Two managers meet the same candidate. One gives five out of five, the other two. Each asked what came to mind and judged by a feeling. The candidate who talks well wins, and three months later the team has a problem. An interview works when everyone asks about the same things, hears evidence instead of opinions and puts the score on one scale.

What changes after this course

You know what you assess before the candidate enters the room. Your questions ask for a real situation, an action and a result. You hear when an answer has no evidence and know how to ask again. Every interviewer fills in the same scorecard, and the final decision compares scores, not impressions. For key roles you add a test task or an assessment center. And candidates get clear feedback, whatever the decision.

What is inside: 340 tools, counted file by file

You do not have to take this number on trust. Open any lecture and read its description: every tool inside is listed there by name.

Who is teaching

I am Mike, the #1 HR instructor on Udemy, with 1,800,000+ course enrollments from 170,000 students, and the author of about 200 books on Amazon. I hold PHRi, SHRM-CP and HCI sHRBP certifications and represent HRCI in Eastern Europe.

When I joined a television channel to build recruiting, I found chaos. Recruiters did not know the assessment criteria. They forwarded resumes and invited people to interviews. About half of the new hires did not pass the probation period. In 2010 I introduced a candidate scorecard there, when it was not yet popular. The first thing it showed was how far apart people were: a recruiter gave one score and the hiring manager a completely different one, or two managers scored the same candidate five and two. That gap is where hiring mistakes come from, and a shared scorecard is how you close it.

You have already tried sleeping more, taking the weekend properly, and putting your phone in another room. It helped for about four days.

Why the usual advice does not work

Because none of it changes the arithmetic. Your workload did not arrive all at once — it accumulated, one reasonable request at a time, and nobody ever went back and renegotiated the total. You are still doing three things you took on temporarily two years ago. You have not handed anything over because the handover would take longer than the task. And underneath all of it there may be a question you have been avoiding, which is whether this is the right job at all. Recovery techniques treat the symptom of that. They are worth having. They are not a solution.

What this course covers

Thirty-five lessons. The mechanism first: what separates stress from burnout, where each comes from, how they are diagnosed, and how organisations measure them — useful because it explains why the environment you are in keeps producing the same result. Then the lever that changes the total: why handing work over is hard, RACI, doing it so it does not come back, and buying your own hours back. Then your own pattern across five frameworks — MBTI, DISC, PAEI, Belbin and Hogan, the Big Five — which is mostly useful for telling "this person is impossible" apart from "this person is built differently". Burnout can shade into depression and anxiety, and those require a qualified professional; nothing here substitutes for that, and recognising when you have crossed that line is part of taking this seriously. Most of what you need to know at work is already known by someone who has no particular reason to tell you.

They are not hiding it. You just have not asked in a way that makes answering worth their while.

Where the information stops

You ask a candidate about a project and get a story that has been told forty times, polished smooth, with the difficult parts sanded off. You ask your team how things are going and get "fine", because the honest answer costs them something and the question cost you nothing. You send a survey and get a response rate of nineteen percent and a set of averages that describe nobody. And you run a 360 that produces a number, a defensive reaction and no change.

The common factor is not honesty. It is that asking well is a technical skill, and almost nobody is taught it.

What the course teaches

Thirty-eight lessons across five ways of finding things out. Emotional intelligence first, eight lessons, because the state you bring into a conversation determines what the other person is prepared to say. Resonance, empathy, reading your own reactions, and the difference between influencing through logic and through emotion.

Then the one-to-one conversation with the highest cost of error: the interview. Question design, STAR, competency maps, active listening in the technical sense of clarifying and interpreting rather than nodding, and how to score what you heard without your own bias doing the work.

Structured questioning, and what to do when questions fail

Then competency-based questioning in depth. Building a question set from what your own best performers actually do, behavioural and situational questions, panel formats, and the CARE technique for getting past a rehearsed answer into what happened. Including how to notice that someone is constructing the story as they speak.

Then asking many people about one person. Eight lessons on the 360: describing observable behaviour instead of traits, writing scales that mean something, evaluator bias, response rates, and delivering the result in a way that produces a development plan rather than a defence.

Then asking in writing and at scale — survey types, question wording, scale choice, the length at which quality collapses, reporting, and turning answers into a plan. And finally the assessment centre, for the cases where asking will never work and you have to watch instead: exercise design, training observers, running the session and validating whether it told you anything.

Mike, the number one HR instructor on Udemy. More than 1.6 million course enrolments, over 150,000 professionals trained, PHRi and SHRM-CP certified, HRCI representative in more than 10 countries.   • Practical assignments and real business cases

After the next answer you get, stay silent for four seconds instead of asking the next question. Most of the useful information in any conversation arrives in the sentence the person adds because the silence was uncomfortable. Enrol now and start the first lesson today.
